rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: The resurrection is easier in the creaturely sense because it follows an initial creation; by this familiar measure, denying God's power to restore is incoherent.
rows.anchor: وهو أيسر عليه، أي أقصر مدة وأقل انتقالا. وقيل: المعنى

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the pronoun in “easier for Him” returns to God; the following statement of God's incomparable supreme attribute supports this reading.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: والأظهر عندي عود الضمير على الله تعالى، ويؤيده قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains that fronting “for Me” in the earlier statement marks exclusivity, whereas delaying it here suits the familiar comparison of return with origination.
rows.anchor: قلت: هنالك قصد الاختصاص، وهو تجبره، فقيل: وهو علي هين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects al-Zamakhsharī's general rule that placing a complement first necessarily signals exclusivity, including its application to “You alone we worship.”
rows.anchor: ومبنى كلامه على أن تقديم المعمول يؤذن بالاختصاص، وقد تكلمنا معه في ذلك،

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj attaches “His is the highest attribute” to the preceding statement; other grammarians attach it to the following parable.
rows.anchor: قيل: هو متعلق بما قبله، قاله الزجاج، وهو قوله: وهو أهون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The supreme attribute is God's unsurpassed description: He can create, restore, and do everything; “Mighty” means dominant over all, and “Wise” means His acts follow wisdom.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المثل: الوصف الأرفع الأعلى الذي ليس لغيره مثله، وهو أنه القادر الذي لا يعجز

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the supreme attribute as “There is no god but God,” affirming divine oneness.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد: المثل الأعلى قوله: لا إله إلا الله، وله الوصف بالوحدانية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others read the parable as an argument against associating idols with God: people do not make their owned slaves equal partners in their property and authority, so they should not claim divine partners.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وغيره: بين تعالى أمر الأصنام وفساد معتقد من يشركها بالله، بضربه هذا المثل

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says the Meccans used to bequeath property to their idols, prompting the revelation.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: كانوا يورثون آلهتهم، فنزلت.

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A report says that when the verse came down, the Meccans said it would never happen, and the Prophet challenged them to explain why they allowed this for their Lord; the author gives no grading.
rows.anchor: قال أهل مكة: لا يكون ذلك أبدا، فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «فلم يجوز لربكم»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the parable, min in “from yourselves” marks origin and closeness, min in “from what your right hands possess” is partitive, and min before “partners” strengthens a rhetorical question functioning as denial.
rows.anchor: ومن في: من أنفسكم لابتداء الغاية، كأنه قال:

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī distinguishes the parable's similarity and difference: humans are limited kin, while God is exalted and powerful; even a slave resembling an owner cannot share the owner's status.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي: وبين المثل والممثل به مشابهة ومخالفة.

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says human slaves remain within human ownership, whereas God's created servants can never leave His ownership; this makes the proposed partnership still less plausible.
rows.anchor: مملوكه تعالى لا خروج له عن الملك.

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says people own provision only nominally, while God is its real giver; if no partner shares what humans nominally own, none can share God's real dominion.
rows.anchor: وقوله: في ما رزقناكم: يعني أن الميسر لكم في الحقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author parses “partners” as a nominative subject and explains the rhetorical question's syntax, including the fronted circumstantial phrase and the clauses describing equality and fear.
rows.anchor: وشركاء في موضع رفع بالابتداء، وفي ما رزقناكم متعلق به، ولكم الخبر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negative force covers the whole proposed relation: because they have no partners, there can be no equality or mutual fear, rather than negating only the final clauses.
rows.anchor: والمقصود نفي الشركة والاستواء والخوف، وليس النفي منسحبا على الجواب

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers recite “yourselves” in the accusative, construing the verbal noun with its agent; Ibn Abī ʿUbayda reads it nominative with the verbal noun construed with its object. The author accepts both.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: أنفسكم، بالنصب، أضيف المصدر إلى الفاعل وابن أبي عبيدة: بالرفع،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In this way We explain the signs” means that parables clarify meanings as pictures do, making the ugliness of idolatry visible.
rows.anchor: كذلك: أي مثل ذلك التفصيل، نفصل الآيات: أي نبينها، لأن التمثيل مما يكشف المعاني ويوضحها،

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers use the first-person plural “We explain,” matching “We provided you”; ʿAbbās ibn ʿUmar reads the third-person “He explains,” matching the preceding mention of the parable.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: نفصل، بالنون، حملا على رزقناكم وعباس عن ابن عمر: بياء الغيبة،

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Some scholars infer that partnership among human equals is sound because people need one another; the objection concerns slaves sharing with their masters.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعض العلماء في هذه الآية دليلا على صحة أصل الشركة بين المخلوقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift to “Rather, the wrongdoers follow” rules out a valid argument or excuse: they follow desire without knowledge, although desire can sometimes be informed.
rows.anchor: ليس لهم حجة ولا معذرة فيما فعلوا من إشراكهم بالله، بل ذلك بمجرد هوى بغير علم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wrongdoers are the polytheists, who follow their desires blindly because they lack knowledge that might restrain them.
rows.anchor: والذين ظلموا: هم المشركون، اتبعوا أهواءهم جاهلين هائمين على أوجههم،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī glosses God's leading astray as abandoning someone without grace, and treats the denial of helpers as evidence for that sense; the author identifies this as a Muʿtazilite approach.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: من أضل الله: من خذله الله ولم يلطف به،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Set your face toward the religion” pictures turning toward Islam with steady attention; the face is named because it gathers the senses and is the noblest part.
rows.anchor: فأقم وجهك للدين: فقوم وجهك له وعدله غير ملتفت، وهو تمثيل لإقباله على الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A true monotheist” may describe the addressee, face, or religion, and means turning away from distorted, superseded religions.
rows.anchor: وحنيفا: حال من الضمير في أقم، أو من الوجه، أو من الدين،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God's fitra” is parsed as a cognate accusative, or as an implicit imperative to keep to the innate disposition; al-Zamakhsharī's “upon you is God's fitra” is rejected because it deletes both the verb and its substitute.
rows.anchor: فطرت الله: منصوب على المصدر، كقوله: صبغة الله

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: The command to set one's face may address the Prophet in singular form while intending the community, which explains the later plural forms.
rows.anchor: وقيل: فأقم وجهك، المراد به: فأقيموا وجوهكم، وليس مخصوصا بالرسول وحده،

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: One explanation identifies fitra with Islam and takes “people” to mean believers; another identifies it with the primordial covenant made with Adam's descendants.
rows.anchor: والفطرة، قيل: دين الإسلام، والناس مخصوصون بالمؤمنين. وقيل: العهد الذي أخذه الله على ذرية آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discerning scholars prefer fitra as the child's innate capacity to reason from God's works to their Maker, believe in Him, and follow His laws; upbringing and devils can divert it.
rows.anchor: ورجح الحذاق. أنها القابلية التي في الطفل للنظر في مصنوعات الله،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No change in God's creation” means the Creator does not alter this innate capacity.
rows.anchor: لا تبديل لخلق الله: أي لا تبديل لهذه القابلية من جهة الخالق.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Nakhaʿī, and Ibn Zayd interpret the phrase as no change to God's religion or its shared principles.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد، وابن جبير، والضحاك، والنخعي، وابن زيد: لا تبديل لدين الله،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the innate disposition should not be replaced or changed.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أي ما ينبغي أن تبدل تلك الفطرة أو تغير.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the phrase as God's decree concerning people's blessedness or wretchedness.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: لا تبديل لقضاء الله بسعادتهم وشقاوتهم،

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: Another reading takes the statement as a prohibition: do not change that religion.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو نفي معناه: النهي، أي لا تبدلوا ذلك الدين.

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says innate monotheism is so deeply rooted that people answer “God” when asked who created the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لا تبديل لخلق الله بمعنى: الوحدانية مترشحة فيه، لا تغير لها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds strange Ibn ʿAbbās's reported interpretation that the phrase prohibits castration of male animals.
rows.anchor: ويستغرب ما روي عن ابن عباس أن معنى لا تبديل لخلق الله: النهي عن خصاء الفحول من الحيوان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The upright religion is described by “qayyim,” an intensive form meaning uprightness, derived by assimilation from qayyūm.
rows.anchor: والقيم: بياء مبالغة، من القيام، بمعنى الاستقامة، ووزنه فعيل، أصله قيوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Turning back to Him” has several transmitted syntactic analyses: a state of the people, of an implied plural command, of the pronoun in “set your face,” or a predicate of an implicit “be.”
rows.anchor: منيبين: حال من الناس، ولا سيما إذا أريد بالناس: المؤمنون، أو من الضمير في: الزموا فطرة الله،

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj similarly explains the singular prophetic address followed by plural forms as including the Prophet's community.
rows.anchor: وكذا زعم الزجاج في: يا أيها النبي إذا طلقتم : أي يا أيها النبي والناس،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural participle may also depend on an implied “be,” as indicated by the following “do not be”; the author presents these as transmitted grammatical options.
rows.anchor: أو على خبر كان مضمرة، أي كونوا منيبين، ويدل عليه قوله بعد ولا تكونوا،

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda identifies the people called polytheists as Jews and Christians.
rows.anchor: من المشركين: من اليهود والنصارى، قاله قتادة.

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the polytheists in this phrase as Jews.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: هم اليهود

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة وعائشة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra and ʿĀʾisha take the phrase to include the people of the qibla; “association” is figurative here because they split into sects.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي هريرة وعائشة: أنهم أهل القبلة، ولفظة الإشراك على هذا تجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning includes everyone who associates partners with God, among the People of the Book and others.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المشركين: كل من أشرك، فيدخل فيهم أهل الكتاب وغيرهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who split their religion divide Islam into rival religions according to their desires; each faction follows the leader who caused its misguidance.
rows.anchor: فرقوا دينهم: أي دين الإسلام وجعلوه أديانا مختلفة لاختلاف أهوائهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each party rejoices in and is captivated by its own doctrine; the straightforward syntax makes “each party” the subject and “rejoicing” its predicate.
rows.anchor: كل حزب: أي منهم فرح بمذهبه مفتون به. والظاهر أن كل حزب مبتدأ وفرحون الخبر.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows “from those who split” to stand apart and parses “rejoicing” as an adjective of “each,” supporting the raised form with Arabic poetic usage.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ويجوز أن يكون من الذين منقطعا مما قبله ومعناه: من المفارقين دينهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author illustrates the competing adjective agreement with cited poetry: one line has a lowered adjective for the group, while another raises it as an adjective of “each.”
rows.anchor: وعليه هبت كل معصفة ... هوجاء ليس للبها دبر برفع هوجاء صفة لكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Harm” includes poverty, illness, drought, or other hardship, while “mercy” is deliverance from it; people call on God alone and abandon idols because they know He alone removes harm.
rows.anchor: الضر: الشدة، من فقر، أو مرض، أو قحط، أو غير ذلك والرحمة: الخلاص من ذلك الضر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After deliverance, some idol-worshippers revert to associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: وإذا خلصهم من ذلك الضر، أشرك فريق ممن خلص، وهذا الفريق هم عبدة الأصنام.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya extends the warning figuratively to believers who credit a created helper or their own cleverness for relief, which shows deficient gratitude.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ويلحق من هذه الألفاظ شيء للمؤمنين، إذ جاءهم فرج بعد شدة،

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī calls it hidden shirk to credit a particular star or idol with deliverance, even when that cause seems evident.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي: يقول: تخلصت بسبب اتصال الكوكب الفلاني وسبب الصنم الفلاني،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first “when” is conditional and the second marks suddenness; “a group” is singular because the verse addresses all people, while only unbelievers associate partners.
rows.anchor: وإذا فريق: جواب إذا أذاقهم، الأولى شرطية، والثانية للمفاجأة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the specific sea peril in the closing verse of al-ʿAnkabūt, the hardship here is general; that verse's context identifies idolaters aboard ships.
rows.anchor: وضر هنا مطلق، وفي آخر العنكبوت إذا هم يشركون لأنه في مخصوصين من المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in “so that they may disbelieve” can mark purpose or function as an imperative of threat, as in the parallel passage at the end of al-ʿAnkabūt.
rows.anchor: واللام في ليكفروا لام كي، أو لام الأمر للتهديد، وتقدم نظيره في آخر العنكبوت.

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya reads the verb with yāʾ in a passive form, coordinated with the preceding purpose clause, and reads the threat “they will know” in the third person.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو العالية: فيتمتعوا، بالياء، مبنيا للمفعول، وهو معطوف على ليكفروا.

rows.speaker: أبو العالية وعبد الله
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya and ʿAbd Allāh transmit further third-person readings, including an imperative threat, while ʿAbd Allāh's codex has “let them be given enjoyment.”
rows.anchor: وعنه وعن عبد الله: فليتمتعوا. وقال هارون في مصحف عبد الله: يمتعوا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Or did We send down authority?” begins a new rebuking, denying question; authority means proof, such as a revealed book, and its “speaking” is figurative unless it means a ruler with evidence.
rows.anchor: والسلطان: البرهان، من كتاب أو نحوه. فهو يتكلم: أي يظهر مذهبهم وينطق بشركهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied question is whether God sent them proof that testifies in favor of their idolatry; a book's speaking is a figure of speech, while a ruler with proof could speak literally.
rows.anchor: بل أنزلنا عليهم سلطانا، أي برهانا شاهدا لكم بالشرك، فهو يشهد بصحة ذلك،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Mercy” means a blessing such as rain, abundance, or health; “misfortune” is a trial such as an event, hardship, or illness caused by their earlier deeds.
rows.anchor: وإذا أذقنا الناس رحمة: أي نعمة، من مطر، أو سعة، أو صحة. وإن تصبهم سيئة: أي بلاء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When blessing arrives people forget gratitude, and when adversity strikes they despair, forget patience, and overlook prior blessings; this follows the principle that God does not change a people until they change themselves.
rows.anchor: إن الله لا يغير ما بقوم حتى يغيروا ما بأنفسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominal clause “they despair” can answer the conditional in place of a fāʾ; the blessing's cause is omitted as gratuitous favor, while sin is named as the cause of adversity.
rows.anchor: جواب: وإن تصبهم، يقوم مقام الفاء في الجملة الاسمية الواقعة جوابا للشرط.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's control of expansion and restriction should keep people from despair and teach patience in hardship, gratitude in ease, and repentance from sins that brought adversity.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر تعالى الأمر الذي من اعتبره لم ييأس من روح الله، وهو أنه تعالى هو الباسط القابض،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to give relatives, the poor, and travelers follows the reminder that God distributes provision: the enriched believer should show compassion and pay the due from wealth.
rows.anchor: ومناسبة فآت ذا القربى لما قبله: أنه لما ذكر أنه تعالى هو الباسط القابض،

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan takes the address as applying to every listener, enjoining care for relatives, the poor, and travelers.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: هذا خطاب لكل سامع بصلة الرحم، والمسكين وابن السبيل.

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: Another view takes the addressee to be the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقيل: للرسول، عليه السلام.

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: One interpretation identifies near relatives as Banū Hāshim and Banū al-Muṭṭalib, entitled to shares from war booty and fayʾ; al-Ḥasan assigns the poor and traveler their specified charity.
rows.anchor: وذو القربى: بنو هاشم وبنو المطلب، يعطون حقوقهم من الغنيمة والفيء.

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa uses the verse to support obligatory maintenance for needy close unmarriageable kin who cannot earn, since it affirms a right for relatives as well as the poor and traveler.
rows.anchor: واحتج أبو حنيفة بهذه الآية في وجوب النفقة للمحارم إذا كانوا محتاجين عاجزين عن الكسب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the sura is Meccan, the right given here is apparently not zakāt but a duty of generosity and mutual aid; relatives come first because their claim is both charity and kinship.
rows.anchor: والسورة مكية، فالظاهر أن الحق ليس الزكاة، وإنما يصير حقا بجهة الإحسان والمواساة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That” refers to the giving, which is better through multiplied afterlife reward and worldly growth when done to seek God's pleasure.
rows.anchor: ذلك: أي الإيتاء، خير: أي يضاعف لهم الأجر في الآخرة، وينمو ما لهم في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Money given as usury to increase wealth does not grow with God or receive blessing; the author links this to the statement that God erases usury and nurtures charity.
rows.anchor: فلا يزكو عند الله، ولا يبارك فيه لقوله: يمحق الله الربا ويربي الصدقات

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says the verse was revealed about Thaqīf's usurious dealings with Quraysh.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: نزلت في ربا ثقيف، كانوا يعملون بالربا، ويعمله فيهم قريش.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, and Ṭāwūs say the verse concerns gifts given in expectation of a return.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وابن جبير، وطاوس: هذه الآية نزلت في هبات، للثواب.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya extends the gift interpretation to similar reciprocal arrangements: they are not sinful but bring no divine reward or increase.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وما جرى مجراهما مما يصنع للمجازاة، كالسلم وغيره، فهو وإن كان لا إثم فيه،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والنخعي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Nakhaʿī interpret the verse as gifts to relatives or brothers intended to benefit and finance them; any increase accrues to the recipients.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا، والنخعي: نزلت في قوم يعطون قراباتهم وإخوانهم على معنى نفعهم

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī gives a similar interpretation: when someone serves another and the other benefits, that benefit belongs to the recipient.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي قريبا من هذا وهو: أن ما خدم به الإنسان غيره انتفع به، فذلك النفع لهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the first interpretation: the passage prohibits usury.
rows.anchor: والظاهر القول الأول، وهو النهي عن الربا.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers lengthen the initial hamza in “what you give,” meaning what you grant; Ibn Kathīr shortens it, meaning what you bring.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: وما آتيتم، الأول بمد الهمزة، أي وما أعطيتم وابن كثير: بقصرها، أي وما جئتم.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read “to increase” with yāʾ, attributing the increase to usury; several authorities read it with feminine tāʾ, attributing it to the gifts, while Abū Mālik adds a feminine object suffix.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: ليربو، بالياء وإسناد الفعل إلى الربا وابن عباس، والحسن، وقتادة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those who multiply” means people whose reward is multiplied; al-Farrāʾ compares the form to words meaning owners of fat or thirsty camels.
rows.anchor: والمضعف: ذو أضعاف في الأجر. قال الفراء: هم أصحاب المضاعفة، كما تقول:

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy reads “the multiplied” with fatḥa on the ʿayn, as a passive participle.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي: المضعفون، بفتح العين، اسم مفعول.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī hears a rhetorical shift to God's angels and chosen creatures, and supplies an omitted complement: the donors are multiplied in reward.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: فأولئك هم المضعفون، التفات حسن، كأنه قال لملائكته وخواص خلقه:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says al-Zamakhsharī's reading is easier to construe, but the first interpretation carries more benefit.
rows.anchor: وهذا أسهل مأخذا، والأول أملأ بالفائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God repeats the challenge to idolaters by listing creation, provision, death, and life—acts that cannot be ascribed to their partners—then rebukes them and declares Himself exalted above their claims.
rows.anchor: كرر تعالى خطاب الكفار في أمر أوثانهم، فذكر أفعاله التي لا يمكن أن يدعى له فيها شريك،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī offers an alternate syntax: “the One who created you” is an adjective of the subject, while the question about partners supplies the predicate; the author disputes his proposed link through “that.”
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ويجوز أن يكون الذي خلقكم صفة للمبتدأ، والخبر: هل من شركائكم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī paraphrases the question as asking whether any idols ever perform even one of these acts; the author objects that “ever” is a past-time adverb used here with a present verb.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري أيضا: هل من شركائكم الذين اتخذتموهم أندادا له من الأصنام وغيرها من يفعل شيئا قط

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī parses the repeated min particles as reinforcing the challenge: the first is partitive, the second introduces the subject, the next marks a circumstantial phrase, and the last is extra under negation.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري أيضا: ومن الأولى والثانية، كل واحدة مستقبلة تأكيد لتعجيز شركائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A conditional expression requires a pronoun in its answer to complete the grammatical link, which motivates the supplied wording in the preceding parsing.
rows.anchor: وإنما احتاج إلى تقدير ما قدر، لأن اسم الشرط ليس بظرف،

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers say “they associate” in the third person; al-Aʿmash and Ibn Waththāb address the audience directly.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: يشركون، بياء الغيبة والأعمش، وابن وثاب: بتاء الخطاب،

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan sees corruption on land and sea in lost blessings, calamities, upheavals, and enemy incursions, all found in both settings.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: وظهور الفساد فيهما بارتفاع البركات، ونزول رزايا، وحدوث فتن،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets corruption on land as highway robbery.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: الفساد في البر، القطاع فتسده.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says land corruption was Cain killing his brother and sea corruption was ships being seized by force; he also offers inland versus coastal and riverbank regions.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: في البر، بقتل أحد بني آدم لأخيه، وفي البحر: بأخذ السفن غصبا،

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda takes “land” as deserts, tribal areas, and rural settlements, and “sea” as cities, citing the expression about the people of al-Buḥayra; Ikrima's plural reading supports this.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: البر: الفيافي ومواضع القبائل وأهل الصحاري والعمور، والبحر: المدن،

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās reports two readings: drought and high prices in inland and coastal cities, or sins such as robbery and injustice as true corruption, with drought only figuratively described.
rows.anchor: وقال النحاس: فيه قولان، أحدهما: ظهر الجدب في البر في البوادي

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says reduced rain curtails diving and harms fishermen; Ibn ʿAbbās says rain opens sea shells and what falls into them becomes pearls.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إذا قل المطر قل الغوص، وأحنق الصياد وعميت دواب البحر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The corruption results from people's sins; God lets them taste some consequences in worldly life before the full punishment, so they may turn back.
rows.anchor: بما كسبت أيدي الناس: أي بسبب معاصيهم وذنوبهم.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the preposition can mean “as recompense for” their deeds or attach directly to the appearance of corruption, which is itself their sinful behavior.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: بما كسبت: جزاء ما كسبت، ويجوز أن يتعلق الباء بظهر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to travel and observe past nations warns Quraysh to learn how God destroyed Noah's people, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and others for sins and idolatry.
rows.anchor: ثم أمرهم بالمسير في الأرض، فينظروا كيف أهلك الأمم بسبب معاصيهم وإشراكهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Most of them were polytheists” may mean all were destroyed for association, while some were destroyed for other sins too, as with the people of the Sabbath.
rows.anchor: أهلكهم كلهم بسبب الشرك، وقوم بسبب المعاصي، لأنه تعالى يهلك بالمعاصي،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that God destroyed all, including believers, as in the warning that a trial can strike wrongdoers and others; alternatively all were unbelievers, most polytheists and some atheists.
rows.anchor: المشرك والمؤمن، كقوله تعالى: واتقوا فتنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage contrasts God's favor, creating people and sustaining them with provision, with their abandonment in transgression through visible corruption and eventual destruction.
rows.anchor: وحين ذكر امتنانه قاله: الله الذي خلقكم ثم رزقكم، فذكر الوجود ثم البقاء بسبب الرزق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coming day is the Resurrection and a warning to everyone; “from God” can mean no one can prevent its arrival, or that God will not turn it away after bringing it.
rows.anchor: من قبل أن يأتي يوم: يوم القيامة، وفيه تحذير يعم الناس، لا مرد له من الله،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that day people split into the Garden's party and the Fire's party; the verb's root evokes division, like a headache that divides the head, as illustrated by poetry.
rows.anchor: يصدعون: يتفرقون، فريق في الجنة، وفريق في السعير. يقال: تصدع القوم إذا تفرقوا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbeliever's fate is expressed with “against him,” signaling burden and hardship, while the believer's benefit is marked with the lām of possession.
rows.anchor: وعبر عن حالة الكافر بعليه، وهي تدل على الفعل والمشقة، وعن حال المؤمن بقوله: فلأنفسهم،

rows.speaker: السلمي
rows.claim: A set of readers, including al-Sulamī and al-Aʿraj, read “that We may make them taste” in the first-person plural; most read it in the third person.
rows.anchor: وقرأ السلمي، والأعرج، وأبو حيوة، وسلام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning corruption and destruction caused by idolatry, God mentions the winds as signs of reform; His generosity needs no justification, while punishment is given a cause to forestall any suspicion of injustice.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر تعالى ظهور الفساد والهلاك بسبب الشرك، ذكر ظهور الصلاح. والكريم لا يذكر لإحسانه عوضا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The winds herald rain because they precede it; winds from the south, north, and east bring mercy, while the west wind brings punishment.
rows.anchor: والمبشرات: رياح الرحمة، الجنوب والشمال والصبا، وأما الدبور، فريح العذاب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their glad tidings also include carrying ships toward their destinations; rain is the greatest sign, bringing fertility, clean air, and winnowed grain.
rows.anchor: وليس تبشيرها مقتصرا به على المطر، بل لها تبشيرات بسبب السفن والسير بها إلى مقاصد أهلها،

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads “the wind” in the singular while intending a collective meaning, as confirmed by the following plural participle.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: الريح، مفردا، وأراد معنى الجمع، ولذلك قرأ: مبشرات.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about letting people taste mercy is linked to the sense of “bearing glad tidings,” perhaps through an understood “so they may be given good news”; other analyses posit an omitted clause or an extra wāw.
rows.anchor: وليذيقكم: عطف على معنى مبشرات، فالعامل أن يرسل، ويكون عطفا على التوهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “By His command” explains that, although the winds are grammatically made agents, their movement is ultimately ordered by God; “of His bounty” includes trade winds and spoils from idolaters.
rows.anchor: وبأمره: أي بأمر الله، يعني أن جريانها، لما كان مسندا إليها، أخبر أنه بأمره تعالى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage turns to prophethood, the third foundational theme after origin and return; some prophets were believed and others denied, after which God avenged the criminals.
rows.anchor: ثم بين لرسوله بأن ضرب له مثل من أرسل من الأنبياء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that aiding believers is incumbent announces victory to the Prophet and his community, honors believers, and presents prior faith as deserving divine support.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: كان حقا علينا نصر المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The subject “the aid of believers” is delayed after its complement to focus attention on the promised result.
rows.anchor: الاسم، وأخر لكون ما تعلق به فاصلة للاهتمام بالجزاء، إذ هو محط الفائدة.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says some readers pause after “a duty” and start a new sentence with “upon Us is the aid of believers”; the author calls this a weak reading of the verse's structure.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وقف بعض القراء على حقا وجعله من الكلام المتقدم، ثم استأنف جملة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī also allows a pause after “a duty,” taking the first clause to mean that taking revenge was deserved and beginning the next clause with God's aid to believers.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وقد يوقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that pause, the destruction is presented as justice rather than injustice because the evildoers' continued existence would produce only more sin and corrupt offspring.
rows.anchor: وفي الوقف على كان حقا بيان أنه لم يكن الانتقام ظلما، بل عدلا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse about God sending winds resumes “Among His signs is that He sends winds”; the intervening sentence comforts the Prophet, promises victory, and warns unbelievers.
rows.anchor: الله الذي يرسل الرياح، هذا متعلق بقوله: ومن آياته أن يرسل الرياح مبشرات،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wind's force shows divine power: delicate air precedes lightning that uproots trees and demolishes buildings, though air itself is not the agent but a voluntary actor is.
rows.anchor: وفي إرسالها قدرة وحكمة. أما القدرة، فإن الهواء اللطيف الذي يسبقه البرق بحيث يقلع الشجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same winds display wisdom by raising clouds, producing rain and crops, nourishing livestock, and distributing these benefits selectively according to God's will.
rows.anchor: وأما الحكمة، ففيما يفضي إليه نفس الهبوب من إثارة السحب، وإخراج الماء منه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Stirring” means moving the clouds, spreading means dispersing them across the horizons, and “pieces” means fragments; the pronoun in “through it” most naturally refers to clouds.
rows.anchor: والبسط: نشرها في الآفاق، والكسف: القطع.

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: The pronoun in “through it” may instead refer to the fragmented cloud in the reading that leaves the relevant consonant unvowelled; “sky” means the direction above.
rows.anchor: قيل: ويحتمل أن يعود على كسفا في قراءة من سكن العين،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When rain reaches the land God chooses, people become joyful at once; al-Akhfash treats “before it” as reinforcing “before it descends.”
rows.anchor: فإذا أصاب به من يشاء: أي أرض من يشاء إصابتها، فاجأهم الاستبشار، ولم يتأخر سرورهم.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the repeated “before it” shows how quickly people move from despair to delight, specifying that the joy follows close upon the rain.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: أفاد الإعلام بسرعة تقلب قلوب البشر من الإبلاس إلى الاستبشار،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the repetition indicates a long drought and settled despair, making their joy proportionate to their prior need.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وبمعنى التوكيد، فيه الدلالة على أن عهدهم بالمطر قد تطاول وبعد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds the proposed implications of “before it” unobvious; the repetition serves emphasis and removes a figurative reading.
rows.anchor: وما ذكره ابن عطية والزمخشري من فائدة التأكيد في قوله: من قبله غير ظاهر، وإنما هو عند ذكره لمجرد التوكيد،

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Quṭrub construes the words as “even before the sending,” meaning before the rain; the author rejects this as unidiomatic.
rows.anchor: وقال قطرب: التقدير: وإن كانوا من قبل التنزيل، من قبل المطر. انتهى.

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: Another proposal supplies “before sowing,” inferred from rain and the later mention of crops turning yellow; the author says the syntax cannot support this attachment.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التقدير: من قبل تنزيل الغيث: من قبل أن يزرعوا، ودل المطر على الزرع،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed attachment to sowing fails because two prepositional phrases cannot depend on the same verb here without coordination or apposition, and rain is neither sowing nor part of it.
rows.anchor: ولا يمكن من قبل الزرع أن يتعلق بمبلسين، لأن حرفي جر لا يتعلقان بعامل واحد

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad takes the pronoun to refer to clouds, but the author notes that this analysis also needs a conjunction to link the two prepositional phrases.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: الثاني السحاب، ويحتاج أيضا إلى حرف عطف حتى يمكن تعلق الحرفين بمبلسين.

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā interprets “before it” as before the sending; al-Kirmānī interprets it as before the glad tidings because it is paired with despair.
rows.anchor: وقال علي بن عيسى: من قبل الإرسال. وقال الكرماني: من قبل الاستبشار، لأنه قرنه بالإبلاس،

rows.speaker: الحرميان
rows.claim: The two Ḥaramayn readers, Abū ʿAmr, and Abū Bakr recite “trace” in the singular; the rest of the Seven use the plural, and Salām changes the initial vowel and stills the thāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحرميان، وأبو عمرو، وأبو بكر: إلى أثر، بالإفراد وباقي السبعة: بالجمع

rows.speaker: الجحدري
rows.claim: Al-Jaḥdarī, Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ, and Abū Ḥaywa read “it revives” with feminine tāʾ referring to mercy; Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads “We revive,” while most use third-person “He revives.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجحدري، وابن السميفع، وأبو حيوة: تحيي، بالتاء للتأنيث، والضمير عائد على الرحمة.

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: The author of al-Lawāmiʿ explains the feminine verb as agreement by association with mercy, valid only when the noun is identical to or related to the implied referent.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب اللوامح: وإنما أنث الأثر لاتصاله بالرحمة إضافة إليها، فاكتسب التأنيث منها،

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinnī analyzes “how He revives” as a circumstantial clause functioning like “reviving”; the author says the analysis deserves reconsideration.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: نحيي، بنون العظمة والجمهور: يحي، بياء الغيبة، والضمير لله،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The One who can revive dead earth can also resurrect people; the statement reasons by analogy from a power already evident in creation.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جني: كيف يحي جملة منصوبة الموضع على الحال حملا على المعنى،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer “we have reached Khurāsān” illustrates a reply whose conditional premise is supplied by context; when the fāʾ can simply coordinate, an omitted condition need not be invented.
rows.anchor: وحقيقتها أنها جواب شرط يدل عليه الكلام، كأنه قال: إن صح ما قلتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You do not know” may mean they neglected seeking and following truth, or that they did not know or recognize resurrection and thus ask for respite in Hell.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لا تعلمون البعث ولا تعرفون به، فصار مصيركم إلى النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “On that day” refers to the day when the unbelievers swear and the people of knowledge answer them.
rows.anchor: فيومئذ: أي يوم إذ، يقع ذلك من إقسام الكفار وقول أولي العلم لهم.

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: The Kūfan readers use the masculine “it benefits” here and in al-Ṭūr; Nāfiʿ agrees in al-Ṭūr, while the rest of the Seven use the feminine.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكوفيون: لا ينفع، بالياء هنا وفي الطول، ووافقهم نافع في الطول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains “they are not asked to make amends” as not being offered a chance to please God with repentance; he distinguishes this from their remaining unsatisfied, citing the matching statement in al-Jāthiya.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: من قولك: استعتبني فلان فأعتبته: أي استرضاني فأرضيته،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the scene's terror means excuses cannot help and no satisfaction is granted; he takes the verb as equivalent to the simple verb ʿataba.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: هذا إخبار عن هول يوم القيامة، وشدة أحواله على الكفرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the form can mean simply “to be displeased,” leaving the unbelievers so ignored that they are unworthy even of being addressed about making amends.
rows.anchor: فيكون استفعل في هذا بمعنى الفعل المجرد، وهو عتب، أي هم من الإهمال وعدم الالتفات إليهم

none: Verse text only; the segment contains no commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fāṭir is a Meccan sura; its opening follows the prior sura's account of the destruction and punishment of polytheist enemies by calling believers to praise and thank God.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية. ولما ذكر تعالى في آخر السورة التي قبلها هلاك المشركين أعداء المؤمنين،

rows.speaker: الضحاك والزهري
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Zuhrī read “He created” as a past verb; Abū al-Faḍl suggests either an omitted relative pronoun or an understood “already,” which the author critiques.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الضحاك والزهري: فطر، جعله فعلا ماضيا ونصب ما بعده.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects omission of a relative pronoun by Basran grammatical standards and prefers an implicit subject, “He created”; fāṭir means bringing the heavens and earth into existence after nonexistence.
rows.anchor: والأحسن عندي أن يكون خبر مبتدأ محذوف، أي هو فطر، وتقدم شرح فاطر السماوات والأرض،

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī maps the praise clauses in earlier suras to immediate blessings, scripture and religious protection, creation and resurrection, and here the lasting blessing of afterlife; splitting heaven and earth lets spirits descend and bodies emerge.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي: الحمد يكون في غالب الأمر على النعمة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī connects the opening to angels receiving the saved, and the author says the sura begins from the previous ending's warning to doubters before turning to the believer's glad tidings.
rows.anchor: فأول هذه السورة متصل بآخر ما مضى، لأن كما فعل بأشياعهم من قبل بيان لانقطاع رجاء

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads “the one making” in the nominative with an understood subject; ʿAbd al-Wārith's report from Abū ʿAmr omits its tanwīn before the accusative “angels.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن: جاعل بالرفع، أي هو جاعل وعبد الوارث عن أبي عمرو: وجاعل رفعا بغير تنوين،

rows.speaker: ابن يعمر وخليد بن نشيط
rows.claim: Ibn Yaʿmar and Khālid ibn Nashīṭ read “made” as a past verb with “angels” accusative, coordinating it with “created”; al-Ḥasan and Ḥumayd read “messengers” with a still s as a Tamīm dialect.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن يعمر، وخليد بن نشيط: جعل فعلا ماضيا، الملائكة نصبا، وذلك بعد قراءته فاطر بألف،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says past-tense “created/made” presents God's uncountable favors, whereas the active participle forms are more naturally attributes of God with past meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وقرىء الذي فطر السموات والأرض وجعل الملائكة.

rows.speaker: السيرافي
rows.claim: Al-Sīrāfī allows “messengers” to be governed by an active participle even with past sense when two nouns cannot be coordinated; Abū ʿAlī instead supplies an implicit verb.
rows.anchor: فمذهب السيرافي أنه منصوب باسم الفاعل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative “angels” can be derived from grammarians who allow a past verb to govern an object, or treated as an appositive; a future reading can also be an appositive.
rows.anchor: وأما من نصب الملائكة فيتخرج على مذهب الكسائي وهشام في جواز إعمال الماضي النصب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels are messengers by revelation and other commands, but not every angel is a messenger; examples include named archangels, alternating angels, just officials, and the angel sent to three tested men.
rows.anchor: ومعنى رسلا بالوحي وغيره من أوامره، ولا يريد جميع الملائكة لأنهم ليسوا كلهم رسلا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Wings” is a paucity plural in form; if its expected abundance plural is unattested, this form can serve for both small and large numbers.
rows.anchor: وأجنحة جمع جناح، صيغة جمع القلة، وقياس جمع الكثرة فيه جنح على وزن فعل،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī parses “two, three, and four” as adjectives of wings and explains their indeclinability through repeated numerical conversion; the author continues to challenge his grammatical argument.
rows.anchor: فقال الزمخشري: مثنى وثلاث ورباع صفات الأجنحة، وإنما لم تنصرف لتكرار العدل فيها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects al-Zamakhsharī's analogy with other numeral adjectives: mere adjectival status does not bar declension, and his comparison overlooks the required conditions.
rows.anchor: لأن مطلق الصفة لم يعدوه علة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the numerals became definite through conversion from indefinite forms, so they are indeclinable for conversion and definiteness; another view attributes it to conversion and adjective status.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: عدلت عن حال التنكير، فتعرفت بالعدل، فهي لا تنصرف للعدل والتعريف،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The famous grammatical view is that the numerals are indeclinable because of conversion and adjectival use; the conversion-plus-definiteness account belongs to some Kufans.
rows.anchor: وهذا الثاني هو المشهور، والأول قول لبعض الكوفيين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense allows angels to have two, three, four, or more wings; a report says Gabriel has six hundred wings, two spanning east to west.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الملك الواحد من صنف له جناحان، وآخر ثلاثة، وآخر أربعة،

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī elaborates on the physical form of wings and refers the reader to his own book, but the author regards the speculation as unhelpful.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: وأخذ الزمخشري يتكلم على كيفية هذه الأجنحة، وعلى صورة الثلاثة

rows.speaker: وقالت فرقة
rows.claim: One group says each side of an angel has two wings, with some angels having three or four per side, since three on one side would seem unbalanced by familiar examples.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: المعنى أن في كل جانب من الملك جناحان، ولبعضهم ثلاثة،

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: Another view says a single angel may have three wings, as some animals do; the author favors the ordinary lexical meaning of wings.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بل هي ثلاثة لواحد، كما يوجد لبعض الحيوانات.

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī allegorizes two wings as angels' upward reception of God's gifts and downward delivery to creatures, with three or four directions for those acting through intermediaries; the author later rejects the reading as non-Arabic.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي: يزيل بحثه في قوله: الحمد لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author calls al-Rāzī's allegory about angelic wings far-fetched and inconsistent with the Arabic meanings of the words.
rows.anchor: وبحثه في هذه، وفي فاطر السماوات والأرض بحث عجيب، وليس على طريقة فهم العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Two, three, four” most naturally describes the wings; another reading treats “winged” as parenthetical and takes the numerals as a circumstantial phrase governed by an implied “they are sent.”
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن مثنى وما بعده من صفات الأجنحة، وقيل: أولي أجنحة معترض، ومثنى حال،

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: Wings make messengers faster in carrying out God's command, crossing in moments distances that would take years on foot, like birds.
rows.anchor: قيل: وإنما جعلهم أولي أجنحة، لأنه لما جعلهم رسلا، جعل لهم أجنحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He increases creation as He wills” reassures those surprised by winged angels: this is no novelty for God's power, and the general wording includes all creation.
rows.anchor: يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء: تقرير لما يقع في النفوس من التعجب والاستغراب من خبر الملائكة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ narrows the increase to adding wings to angels.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: هذا في الأجنحة التي للملائكة، أي يزيد في خلق الملائكة الأجنحة.

rows.speaker: وقيل
rows.claim: Interpreters list examples of added beauty or gifts—voice, handwriting, features, intelligence, knowledge, skill, chastity, and more—but the author says these are examples rather than an exhaustive restriction.
rows.anchor: وقالوا: في هذه الزيادة الخلق الحسن، أو حسن الصوت، أو حسن الخط،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Any mercy” includes every sort of blessing, such as provision, rain, health, or security; specific early interpretations are examples, since the wording is general.
rows.anchor: من رحمة: أي نعمة ورزق، أو مطر، أو صحة، أو أمن، أو غير ذلك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the indefinite “mercy” deliberately leaves the type open: no one can withhold any heavenly or earthly grace, nor release what God withholds.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: وتنكير الرحمة للإشاعة والإبهام، كأنه قال: من أية رحمة كانت سماوية أو أرضية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional noun makes the meaning general; “what He withholds” also stays general beyond mercy, and the masculine or feminine pronouns can follow either the grammatical form or the meaning.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: وما يمسك عام في الرحمة وفي غيرها، لأنه لم يذكر له تبيين،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading “there is none to release it” with feminine pronoun supports construing the general reference as mercy elided after its earlier mention.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: فلا مرسل لها، بتأنيث الضمير، وهو دليل على أن التفسير هو من رحمة،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets mercy as the opening of repentance: when God opens it no one can close it, and when He withholds it none can open it; he also glosses mercy as guidance.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: من رحمة: من باب توبة، فلا ممسك لها: أي يتوبون إن شاؤوا وإن أبوا،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī accepts repentance if Ibn ʿAbbās means guidance and divine enabling, but rejects the idea that God may choose not to will a sinner's repentance, reflecting Muʿtazilite doctrine.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: فما تقول فيمن فسر الرحمة بالتوبة وعزاه إلى ابن عباس؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “After Him” supplies an omitted noun, meaning after God's withholding; the author rejects al-Zamakhsharī's “after God's guidance” as contrary to the context and Muʿtazilite in method.
rows.anchor: من بعده: هو على حذف مضاف، أي من بعد إمساكه، كقوله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is Mighty in His power to release or withhold, and Wise in sending or withholding what His wisdom requires.
rows.anchor: وهو العزيز الغالب القادر على الإرسال والإمساك، الحكيم الذي يرسل ويمسك ما اقتضته حكمته.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address about God's favors targets Quraysh but reaches believers and unbelievers, especially those worshipping other than God; remembering means preserving and thanking the favor with heart and tongue, not merely verbal mention.
rows.anchor: يا أيها الناس: خطاب لقريش، وهو متجه لكل مؤمن وكافر، ولا سيما من عبد غير الله،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question “Is there any creator besides God?” means that only the Creator deserves worship; the idols worshipped by the addressees create nothing.
rows.anchor: واذكروا: ليس أمرا بذكر اللسان، ولكن به وبالقلب وبحفظ النعمة من كفرانها وشكرها،

rows.speaker: ابن وثاب
rows.claim: Ibn Waththāb, Shaqīq, Abū Jaʿfar, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read “other than” in the genitive, as an adjective agreeing by form.
rows.anchor: هل من خالق غير الله: أي فلا إله إلا الخالق، ما تعبدون أنتم من الأصنام.

rows.speaker: شيبة
rows.claim: Shayba, ʿĪsā, al-Ḥasan, and the rest of the Seven read “other than” in the nominative; it can agree by semantic position, stand as predicate, or serve as the active participle's subject, though the author questions the last parse.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن وثاب، وشقيق، وأبو جعفر، وزيد بن علي، وحمزة، والكسائي: غير بالخفض،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author doubts that an active participle after an interrogative can take a universal min phrase before its subject, since he knows no such construction in Arabic.
rows.anchor: وقرأ شيبة، وعيسى، والحسن، وباقي السبعة: غير بالرفع، وجوزوا أن يكون نعتا على الموضع،

rows.speaker: الفضل بن إبراهيم
rows.claim: Al-Faḍl ibn Ibrāhīm reads “other than God” in the accusative as an exception; the predicate may be “provides for you” or omitted, and the author favors a resumed verb to avoid implying another creator.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الفضل بن إبراهيم النحوي: غير بالنصب على الاستثناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From heaven” means rain and “from earth” means vegetation; “there is no god but Him” is an independent sentence.
rows.anchor: ومعنى من السماء: بالمطر، والأرض: بالنبات، لا إله إلا هو: جملة مستقلة لا موضع لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “How then are you turned away?” asks how people move from monotheism to idolatry; the earlier discussion of being denied has already been given.
rows.anchor: فأنى تؤفكون: أي كيف يصرفون على التوحيد إلى الشرك، وأن يكذبوك إلى الأمور،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's promise is true and encompasses every promise of reward, punishment, and more.
rows.anchor: إن وعد الله حق: شامل لجميع ما وعد من ثواب وعقاب وغير ذلك.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets “the deceiver” as Satan; a variant reading with ḍamma can mean deceivers or function as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: الغرور بفتح الغين، وفسره ابن عباس بالشيطان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's enmity began with Adam and is shown by his vow to mislead Adam's descendants; people should treat him as an enemy by opposing him and following the revealed law.
rows.anchor: إن الشيطان لكم عدو: عداوته سبقت لأبينا آدم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan calls his party toward punishment in Hell and wants shared suffering, which can console him more than suffering alone; the text then contrasts the two groups' outcomes.
rows.anchor: ثم بين أن مقصوده في دعاء حزبه إنما هو تعذيبهم في النار،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbelievers are mentioned first because they follow the reference to Satan's party; both groups are syntactically independent clauses.
rows.anchor: وبدأ بالكفار لمجاورة قوله: إنما يدعوا حزبه،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the lām in “so that they become” consequential: Satan did not explicitly summon them to Hell, but his call happened to lead there.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: واللام في ليكون لام الصيرورة، لأنه لم يدعهم إلى السعير،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author instead describes the cause by the outcome it produces: Satan's invitation to disbelief causes the punishment.
rows.anchor: ونقول: هو مما عبر فيه عن السبب بما تسبب عنه دعاؤهم إلى الكفر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative parses that make “those who disbelieved” an appositive to several different phrases damage the division and eloquence of the construction.
rows.anchor: وهذا كله بمعزل من فصاحة التقسيم وجزالة التركيب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about one whose evil deed is made attractive means that he sees his bad conduct as good; “whoever” is the relative subject with an omitted predicate.
rows.anchor: أفمن زين له سوء عمله فرآه حسنا: أي فرأى سوء عمله حسنا،
